results.title: Informal introduction to factorial experimental designs - Center for Advancement and Dissemination of Intervention Optimization
results.content: The purpose of this page is to clarify some concepts, notation, and terminology related to factorial experimental designs, and to compare and contrast factorial experiments to randomized controlled trials (RCTs). There is also a factorial experiment FAQ and a page that examines misconceptions about factorial experiments. Because there are three factors and each factor has two levels, this is a 2×2×2, or 23, factorial design. When a design is denoted a 23 factorial, this identifies the number of factors (3); how many levels each factor has (2); and how many experimental conditions there are in the design (23=8). ## Differences between factorial experiments and RCTs. In an RCT there are a very limited number of experimental conditions (“arms” in RCT terminology)—usually just two or three—and the objective is to compare the individual experimental conditions to each other directly. For example, when the main effect of keeping a food diary is estimated, the subjects in experimental conditions 3 and 4 are in the No level.

results.title: Isotope fractionation | Geochemistry Class Notes
results.content: ## 3.3 Isotope fractionation. # 3.3 Isotope fractionation. Isotope fractionation is a key concept in geochemistry, shaping how isotopes distribute in Earth systems. Understanding fractionation is crucial for interpreting isotopic signatures in geological materials. ## Principles of isotope fractionation. * Isotope fractionation fundamentally shapes the distribution of isotopes in geological systems. * Involves the separation of isotopes during physical, chemical, or biological processes. * Kinetic fractionation often produces larger isotope effects and is sensitive to reaction rates. * Occurs due to differences in mass between isotopes of an element. ## Isotope fractionation processes. * Isotope fractionation occurs through various natural and anthropogenic processes. * Understanding these processes is crucial for interpreting isotopic signatures in geochemistry. * Temperature significantly influences equilibrium isotope fractionation. * Pressure can affect isotope fractionation, especially in high-pressure geological environments. * Fractionation factors quantify the extent of isotope separation between two phases or compounds. * Essential for interpreting isotopic data and modeling geochemical processes. * Represents the relative difference in isotope ratios between a sample and a standard. * Allows for comparison of isotopic compositions across different laboratories and studies. ## Isotope systems in geochemistry. * Isotope systems provide powerful tools for investigating geological processes and Earth history. * Different isotope systems offer unique insights into various aspects of the Earth system. * Precise measurement of isotope ratios requires sophisticated analytical techniques. * Gas Source Mass Spectrometry for light stable isotope analysis (carbon, oxygen, nitrogen). * Utilizes temperature-dependent isotope fractionation to estimate formation temperatures. * Radiogenic isotope systems provide absolute ages for rocks and minerals. ## Modeling isotope fractionation. * Mathematical models help interpret and predict isotope fractionation patterns. * Describes isotope fractionation in systems with continuous removal of the product. * Expressed as $R = R\_0 \* f^(α-1)$, where R is the isotope ratio and f is the fraction remaining. * Models isotope fractionation in closed systems at equilibrium. * Understanding the limitations of isotope geochemistry is crucial for accurate interpretations. * Precision varies among different isotope systems and analytical methods. * Particularly challenging for trace element isotope systems and small samples. * Requires careful consideration of geological context and multiple isotope systems.
